note: Typical mistakes are tendencies, not rules about people. They happen because your first language has different sounds, letters or rules: this is called transfer (or interference). Not everyone makes these mistakes, and many learners stop making them quite quickly. If you know where a mistake comes from, you get rid of it faster. Based on comparing the language systems (contrastive linguistics) and on experience from language teaching. Spanish speakers have their own set (interference between two close languages); Romanian, Arabic, Russian, Ukrainian and Chinese carry only the grammar mistakes we are sure of.

languages.name: English
strengths: English and Italian share thousands of words from Latin: family → famiglia, important → importante, hospital → ospedale.
Italian is spelled almost as it is said: once you know the few rules (c/g, gn, gli, sc), you can read any word aloud.

mistakes.wrong: sete and sette, nono and nonno: the same short consonant
mistakes.right: sete: short t · sette: hold the tt
mistakes.why: English has no long consonants inside a word: a double letter only changes the vowel before it. In Italian the consonant itself is held, about twice as long, and it changes the word: caro/carro, sete/sette.

mistakes.right: bene, italiano: every vowel pure, the last one too
mistakes.why: In English, weak syllables turn into a short “uh” (/ə/), and e and o glide into “ay” and “ow”. Italian vowels keep their full, pure sound in every syllable, also the last.

mistakes.wrong: caro, carro with an English r (tongue curled back, no tap)
mistakes.right: caro: one tap · carro: several taps
mistakes.why: English r doesn't touch the top of the mouth. Italian r does: one quick tap for r, a little like the tt in American “butter”, and a trill for rr.
At the start of a stressed syllable, English p, t, k come with a puff of air. Italian p, t, k have none, so the puff sounds foreign straight away.

mistakes.wrong: ho, hanno with a breathy h: “hoh”, “HAN-no”
mistakes.why: In English h is always pronounced. In Italian the letter is silent: it only keeps ho, hai, ha, hanno apart from o, ai, a, anno.

mistakes.right: figlio, bagno: gli and gn are one sound each
mistakes.why: English reads g + l and g + n as two sounds. Italian gli (like lli in “million”) and gn (like ny in “canyon”) are one sound each, and they are long between vowels.

mistakes.wrong: “ZEE-ro”, “PEET-za” with an English z or sharp ts
mistakes.why: English z is only a buzz. Italian z is a ts or a dz, a stop and a hiss together: zio is “TSEE-o”, zero is “DZEH-ro”.
In Italian ch before e or i is /k/ and gh is /g/: the h makes the sound hard. Without the h, ce and ci are the “church” sounds.
sch is always s + k. Only sce and sci (scena, sci) have the sh of “ship”.

mistakes.wrong: smettere, sbaglio with a sharp s: “SMET-te-re”
mistakes.right: smettere: s is voiced, like z in “zoo”
mistakes.why: Before b, d, g, l, m, n, r and v, Italian s is voiced. English keeps it sharp in smell, snow, sleep.
English says I am 25. Italian says I have 25 years: ho 25 anni. It's the same with ho fame, ho sete, ho freddo, ho caldo.

mistakes.wrong: Io sono fame. Io sono freddo.
mistakes.why: In English, hunger and cold are things you are. In Italian they are things you have: ho fame, ho sete, ho freddo, ho caldo. Sono freddo would mean you are a cold person.
piacere works the other way round: literally, the books are pleasing to me. So the verb agrees with the books: mi piace il caffè, mi piacciono i libri.
English always uses have for the perfect. In Italian, verbs of movement (andare, venire, partire, uscire, arrivare) take essere: sono andato, sono venuta.

mistakes.wrong: Io parlo italiano. Io abito a Roma. Io lavoro qui.
mistakes.right: Parlo italiano. Abito a Roma. Lavoro qui.
mistakes.why: English needs I, but in Italian the verb ending already shows the person. You only add io for emphasis or contrast: Io parlo italiano, tu parli inglese.
How you are, in health and mood, goes with stare: sto bene, sto male. Sono bene doesn't exist. Sono is for what you are: sono stanco, sono italiano.
English makes a decision; Italian takes it: prendere una decisione. Learn the pairs: fare una domanda, prendere una decisione, fare un errore, passare il tempo.

mistakes.wrong: Ho speso due ore a studiare.
mistakes.right: Ho passato due ore a studiare.
mistakes.why: Italian spends money (spendere soldi) but passes time (passare il tempo). It's a common mistake for English speakers.
English capitalises languages, nationalities, days and months. Italian doesn't: italiano, inglese, lunedì, gennaio. Only the first word of a sentence and names take a capital.

languages.name: German
strengths: German already has the sounds sch and ts (z), and a clear difference between short and long vowels.
Italian is spelled almost as it is said: once you know c/g, gn, gli and sc, you can read any word aloud.

mistakes.right: studente, sport, stazione: a clean s before t and p
mistakes.why: At the start of a word, German st and sp are “scht” and “schp”. Italian s stays /s/ here: it is only voiced before b, d, g, l, m, n, r, v.
German ch is a hiss (/x/ or /ç/). Italian ch before e or i is only /k/. And c before e, i is not German “ts” but like ch in “church”.
German reads sc as “sts” and sch as “sh”. Italian sce and sci are /ʃ/, but sche and schi are /sk/.

mistakes.wrong: nono and nonno, sete and sette: the same
mistakes.right: nono: short n · nonno: hold the nn
mistakes.why: In German a double letter only shows that the vowel before it is short. In Italian the consonant itself is held, about twice as long, and it changes the word.

mistakes.wrong: parte, carro with the German throat r, or a vowel-like r (“paate”)
mistakes.right: parte: a tongue-tip tap · carro: a trill
mistakes.why: German r is made in the throat and after a vowel it turns into a vowel. Italian r is always a consonant made with the tip of the tongue: one tap, or a trill for rr.
German p, t, k at the start of a stressed syllable come with a puff of air. Italian ones don't.

mistakes.wrong: ho, hanno with a breathy h, as in German haben
mistakes.why: German h is pronounced. In Italian it is silent: it only keeps ho, hai, ha, hanno apart from o, ai, a, anno.

mistakes.right: bene, fame: the last e is a clear “eh”
mistakes.why: In German an unstressed e is a weak “uh”. In Italian every vowel is full, including the last one.
German says Ich bin 25 Jahre alt. Italian says I have 25 years: ho 25 anni.

mistakes.wrong: Il film ha cominciato alle otto.
mistakes.right: Il film è cominciato alle otto.
mistakes.why: German uses haben with anfangen in both cases. In Italian, cominciare and finire take essere when there is no object (il film è cominciato) and avere when there is one (ho cominciato il lavoro).
German warten auf needs a preposition; Italian aspettare takes its object directly: aspetto l'autobus, ti aspetto.

mistakes.right: Non ho niente. Non vedo nessuno.
mistakes.why: German has no double negative (ich habe nichts). Italian does: when niente, nessuno or mai come after the verb, you need non before it: non ho niente, non vedo nessuno.

German says mein Buch; Italian puts the article before the possessive: il mio libro, la mia casa. Exception: a singular family member needs none: mia madre, mio fratello (but: i miei fratelli, la mia amica).
Voglio sounds like a demand. German speakers say ich möchte, so use vorrei (I would like) or Prendo un caffè when you order or ask for something.

mistakes.wrong: Ho comprato una Casa a Roma e un Computer.
mistakes.right: Ho comprato una casa a Roma e un computer.
mistakes.why: German writes every noun with a capital letter. Italian doesn't: only names, places and the first word of a sentence.

languages.name: French
strengths: French and Italian are close relatives: thousands of words look and mean almost the same (famille → famiglia, hôpital → ospedale).
French gn is the same sound as Italian gn (montagne → montagna).

mistakes.wrong: sete and sette, nono and nonno: the same
mistakes.right: sete: short t · sette: hold the tt
mistakes.why: French has no long consonants: a double letter is said like a single one. In Italian the consonant is held about twice as long, and it changes the word.

mistakes.wrong: carro, rosso with the French r (back of the tongue)
mistakes.right: caro: one tap · carro: a trill
mistakes.why: French r is made at the back of the mouth. Italian r is a tap, or for rr a trill, made with the tip of the tongue behind the top teeth.

mistakes.right: bambino, pane, tempo: a clean vowel, then a real m or n
mistakes.why: French has nasal vowels. Italian has none: the vowel stays clean and the n or m is said as a consonant.
In French the stress falls on the last syllable of a phrase. In Italian every word has its own stress: usually the second-to-last, sometimes the third-to-last.

mistakes.wrong: tu, luna with the French u (lips round, tongue forward)
mistakes.right: tu, luna: u as in French “ou” (vous)
mistakes.why: Italian u is a back vowel, like French ou. The French u of “tu” doesn't exist in Italian.

mistakes.right: fame, sera: say the last e
mistakes.why: In French a final unaccented e is silent. In Italian every final vowel is spoken, because it shows gender and number.

mistakes.wrong: giorno, gelato with the French j (“zhorno”)
mistakes.why: Italian g before e or i is /dʒ/, a stop plus a hiss. French j is /ʒ/ with no stop.

mistakes.wrong: Io parlo italiano. Io abito a Parigi. Io lavoro qui.
mistakes.right: Parlo italiano. Abito a Parigi. Lavoro qui.
mistakes.why: French needs the subject (je). In Italian the verb ending shows the person, and io is only for emphasis.

mistakes.wrong: La mare è calma. La fiore è rosso.
mistakes.right: Il mare è calmo. Il fiore è rosso.
mistakes.why: Some words change gender from French to Italian: la mer → il mare, la fleur → il fiore, la dent → il dente, le soir → la sera. Learn the article with every word.
French says mon livre; Italian says il mio libro, with the article. Exception: a singular family member needs none: mia madre, mio fratello.
French tout le monde means everybody. In Italian il mondo is the world, so tutto il mondo = the whole world. Everybody is tutti or tutte le persone.
The accent in perché, città, così, perciò is part of the spelling and is never left out, also when you type fast.

languages.name: Portuguese
strengths: Portuguese nh and lh are the same sounds as Italian gn and gli: sonho → sogno, filho → figlio.
Portuguese and Italian share most of their vocabulary: casa, família → famiglia, importante.

mistakes.right: fame, bene, vino: final e and o are clear
mistakes.why: In Brazilian Portuguese an unstressed final e and o sound like i and u. In Italian they stay e and o, always.

mistakes.wrong: sete and sette, nono and nonno: the same
mistakes.right: sete: short t · sette: hold the tt
mistakes.why: Portuguese has no long consonants. In Italian a double consonant is held about twice as long and changes the word.

mistakes.right: tipo, dire: a plain t and d
mistakes.why: In Brazilian Portuguese t and d before i sound like ch and j. In Italian they stay plain /t/ and /d/.

mistakes.wrong: rosso, carro with a throaty or breathy r (“HOS-so”)
mistakes.right: rosso: a trill with the tongue tip
mistakes.why: A Portuguese r at the start of a word, and rr, is made in the throat. Italian rr is a trill made with the tip of the tongue.

mistakes.right: pane, bambino: a clean vowel, then a real n or m
mistakes.why: Portuguese has nasal vowels. Italian has none: the vowel stays clean and n or m is a consonant.
Portuguese ch is /ʃ/, but Italian ch is /k/. And Italian g before e or i is /dʒ/ (a stop plus a hiss), not /ʒ/.

mistakes.right: questo, sport, studente: a clean s
mistakes.why: In Rio and in Portugal s before a consonant sounds like sh, and Portuguese has an e in front of s + consonant (estudante). Italian s stays /s/ and nothing goes in front of it.
Portuguese moro em Roma uses one preposition for all places. In Italian, cities take a (a Roma, a Milano), countries and regions take in (in Italia, in Sicilia).
Italian merges the preposition with the article: a + il = al, di + il = del, in + il = nel, su + il = sul. Portuguese does the same (ao, do, no), but Italian forms are different and are required.
Italian says andare a + infinitive: vado a fare la spesa. Portuguese vou fazer has no a. In Italian the a is required: vado a mangiare, vado a trovare mia nonna.

mistakes.wrong: La ponte è vecchia. La fiore è bella.
mistakes.right: Il ponte è vecchio. Il fiore è bello.
mistakes.why: Some words have another gender than in Portuguese: a ponte → il ponte, a flor → il fiore, a árvore → l'albero. Learn the article with every word.
Portuguese gosto de makes you the subject. Italian piacere works the other way round: the pizza is pleasing to me. Mi piace la pizza, mi piacciono le patate.

mistakes.wrong: Dopo il lavoro vado in montanha con la mia compania.
mistakes.right: Dopo il lavoro vado in montagna con la mia compagnia.
mistakes.why: Portuguese nh is Italian gn (montanha → montagna), and lh is gli (filho → figlio). The words are alike, so check the spelling.

languages.name: Spanish
strengths: Spanish and Italian share a lot of vocabulary and grammar, and both have five clean vowels.
Spanish r and rr are the same tap and trill as in Italian: pero/perro, caro/carro.

mistakes.wrong: cena, ciao with /θ/ or s (“THEH-na”); gente, giorno with /x/ (“HEN-te”)
mistakes.why: Spanish c before e, i is /θ/ or s, and g before e, i is a rasp /x/. In Italian they are the sounds of ch in “church” and j in “jam”.

mistakes.wrong: che, chi, perché with the Spanish ch: “chay”, “chee”
mistakes.why: Spanish ch is /tʃ/. Italian ch is /k/ and gh is /g/: the h makes c and g hard. Many Spanish speakers mix this up with their own spelling.

mistakes.wrong: sete and sette, nono and nonno: the same
mistakes.right: sete: short t · sette: hold the tt
mistakes.why: Spanish has no long consonants. In Italian a double consonant is held about twice as long and changes the word.

mistakes.right: figlio: one long “lli” sound, like in “million”
mistakes.why: In most Spanish, ll sounds like y. Italian gli is a different sound, with the tongue pressed against the roof of the mouth, and it is long between vowels.

mistakes.right: vino: the top teeth touch your lower lip
mistakes.why: In Spanish b and v are one sound. In Italian v is a separate sound made with teeth and lip: bene (well) and vene (veins) are different words.

mistakes.wrong: pizza, zio with Spanish z: “PEE-tha”, “THEE-o” (or s)
mistakes.why: Spanish z is /θ/ or s. Italian z is ts or dz, the tongue at the teeth with a hiss.
In Spanish the u of que and qui is silent. In Italian qu is k + w: you say the u.

mistakes.right: scuola, studente, sbaglio: start straight on s
mistakes.why: Spanish does not allow s + consonant at the start of a word, so it adds an e (escuela, estudiante). Italian words start straight with s.

mistakes.wrong: è and e, bene and bella with the same Spanish e
mistakes.right: è (is): open · e (and) and perché: closed
mistakes.why: Spanish has one e and one o. In Italian stressed e and o have an open and a closed sound, and a few words depend on it (e/è, pèsca/pésca). Learn the accented words by ear.
Spanish uses a before a person who is the object: veo a Marco. Italian doesn't: vedo Marco, conosco Anna, aspetto mia sorella.
Spanish uses haber for every perfect: he ido. In Italian, verbs of movement and some others take essere: sono andato, sono venuta, sono stato.
Spanish says mi libro. Italian puts the article before the possessive: il mio libro, la mia casa. Not with a singular family member: mia madre, mio fratello.
Spanish hay = Italian c'è (one) or ci sono (more than one). Ha is the verb avere: he/she has.

Spanish says ayer comí (pretérito). In everyday Italian, especially in the north and centre, you use the passato prossimo (ho mangiato) for the recent past. The passato remoto (mangiai) is used for far-away events, and more in speech in the south.
Spanish tengo ganas de = Italian ho voglia di. The word ganas doesn't exist in Italian.

mistakes.wrong: Il mio compañero di lavoro è simpatico.
mistakes.right: Il mio compagno di lavoro è simpatico.
mistakes.why: Spanish ñ = Italian gn (compañero → compagno, España → Spagna), and ll often = gli or li (llamar → chiamare). There is no ñ in Italian.

languages.name: Romanian
strengths: Romanian is a Romance language too, and many words are close: casă – casa, carne – carne, apă – acqua.
The verb ending shows the person, so you can leave out the subject, as in Italian: vorbesc – parlo.
You say I like something the same way: îmi place cafeaua – mi piace il caffè.

mistakes.wrong: Ho comprato una carta alla libreria.
mistakes.right: Ho comprato un libro alla libreria.
mistakes.why: Romanian carte = il libro. In Italian la carta is paper, or a card: la carta d'identità.
Romanian adds the article at the end of the word: omul. In Italian it's a separate word in front: l'uomo, il libro, la casa.
Romanian has one verb, a fi (sunt bine). Italian uses stare for how you are: sto bene, sto male, and essere for what you are.
Romanian says vreau să merg. When both verbs have the same subject, Italian uses the infinitive: voglio andare.

languages.name: Arabic
strengths: Italian has hundreds of words from Arabic: zucchero, arancia, magazzino, algebra, caffè.
The verb ending shows the person, so you can often leave out the subject: parlo, parli, parla.
Italian is written almost as it is said: once you know the few rules (c/g, gn, gli, sc), you can read any word aloud.

mistakes.why: Arabic script has no capital letters. In Italian the first word of a sentence and the names of people and places start with a capital letter.
Arabic has a definite article (al-) but no indefinite one. Italian needs un, uno, una before a singular noun: ho una macchina.
In Arabic there's no verb to be in the present: ana talib. Italian always needs it: sono studente, sei, è, siamo.
In Italian the article and the possessive agree with the noun's gender: la mia casa, il mio libro. Learn the article with every word.

languages.name: Russian
strengths: Nouns have a gender and verbs change for the person, so neither idea is new to you.
Stress is free in Russian and in Italian: you learn it with every word (capitano, càpitano).
Russian has a rolled r like Italian: caro, carro.

mistakes.why: Russian has no articles. Italian needs il, la, un, una: ho comprato una macchina, la macchina è nuova.
Russian leaves out the verb to be in the present (ya student). Italian always says it: sono studente.
Russian u menya yest' = Italian ho. Don't translate word for word: say ho un fratello, ho due figli.
Russian dom is masculine, but Italian casa is feminine, so: la mia casa. Learn the article with every word.

languages.name: Ukrainian
strengths: Nouns have a gender and verbs change for the person, so neither idea is new to you.
A yes/no question can be made with the voice alone, as in Italian: Ти хочеш чаю? – Vuoi un tè?
Ukrainian has a rolled r like Italian: caro, carro.

mistakes.why: Ukrainian has no articles. Italian needs il, la, un, una: ho comprato una macchina.
Ukrainian leaves out the verb to be in the present (ya student). Italian always says it: sono studente.
Ukrainian u mene ye = Italian ho. Say ho una sorella, ho due figli.
Ukrainian dim is masculine, but Italian casa is feminine, so: la mia casa. Learn the article with every word.

languages.name: Chinese
strengths: Like Italian, Chinese puts the subject first, then the verb, then the object: 我喝咖啡 – Bevo il caffè.
Chinese often leaves out I when it's clear, and Italian does that all the time: Ho fame, Vado a casa.
Italian spelling is regular, so reading aloud is easier than in English or French.

mistakes.why: Chinese verbs don't change for time or person. Italian verbs do: the ending and the tense show who and when: vado, sono andato, andrò.
Chinese has no articles. Italian needs un, uno, una (or il, lo, la) before a singular noun.
Chinese words don't change for gender. In Italian the article, the possessive and the adjective agree with the noun: la mia amica italiana.
Chinese nouns stay the same in the plural. In Italian the ending changes: un libro, due libri; una casa, due case.

quiz.prompt: How do you say your age correctly?
quiz.explain: Sono 25 anni comes from English or German. Italian uses avere: ho 25 anni.

quiz.prompt: What does camera mean in Italian?
quiz.explain: A false friend for English speakers. The device is la macchina fotografica or la fotocamera.

quiz.prompt: You like books. What do you say?
quiz.explain: piacere agrees with the thing you like. Io piaccio i libri would mean the books like you.
Verbs of movement take essere in the passato prossimo: sono andato, sono venuta.

quiz.prompt: You feel cold. What do you say?
quiz.explain: How your body feels goes with avere. It's the same in French (j'ai froid), Spanish (tengo frío) and Portuguese (tenho frio).

quiz.prompt: Why do many learners with Arabic as their first language write names with a small letter?
options: Their script has no capital letters
In Arabic everything is written in capitals
quiz.answer: Their script has no capital letters
quiz.explain: In Italian, names and the first word of a sentence start with a capital letter.
A false friend for Spanish speakers: burro = donkey in Spanish. The Italian animal is l'asino.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between caro and carro?
options: One tap of the tongue or several
quiz.answer: One tap of the tongue or several
quiz.explain: caro has one quick tap, and carro has several. They are different words (dear / cart).

quiz.prompt: You moved here three years ago and you still live here. What is correct?
quiz.explain: A length of time that is still going on: da + present. per + a length of time is for something finished.
A false friend for German speakers: die Tasche = la borsa. The Italian tasca is the pocket of a jacket or trousers.
